title: The Disappearing Priority Band: Administrative Downgrades on Housing Registers
setting:
Khadija Al-Hassan and her two children have lived in temporary accommodation for four years following a no-fault eviction. Under her council's allocations scheme, she was placed in Priority Band 1 (Urgent Homelessness with Severe Medical Need), reflecting her daughter's chronic respiratory illness aggravated by damp temporary housing. Bidding each week on the council's choice-based lettings portal, she was consistently in the top three for local two-bedroom tenancies. Then, overnight, her portal position dropped to 140th: an automated data clean-up job downgraded her application to Band 3 (General Need) without a written notification, reasoned decision, or statutory review offer.

In the real system, local authorities under immense housing pressures conduct periodic batch re-assessments and automated purging of priority queues. Tens of thousands of vulnerable households discover priority downgrades only when bids fail. Because the downgrade occurs quietly as a database update rather than a formal decision letter, statutory review deadlines (Housing Act 1996 s.202) elapse before families know there is anything to challenge.

Oakhaven Housing Authority pilots a transparency log where every change in applicant banding, priority points, or queue status must be committed as a signed event citing the statutory medical assessment or housing review. This scenario follows Khadija's challenge to an automated batch downgrade, demonstrating how a verifiable log makes administrative rationing legible while acknowledging the unyielding physical limit: a protocol can guarantee fair queuing, but cannot build more homes.

precedents.event: Housing Act 1996 Part VI, statutory reasonable preference and review rights
precedents.source: Housing Act 1996 ss.166A, 202 (as amended by Localism Act 2011)
precedents.shows: Local authorities must secure reasonable preference for homeless and medical-need applicants and provide written reasons and statutory review rights on adverse allocation decisions.

precedents.event: Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman housing allocation backlog and band-removal investigations
precedents.source: Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman Public Interest Reports
precedents.shows: Ombudsman investigations into major urban councils revealed thousands of applicants silently stuck or downgraded during IT migrations and backlog clearances without required individual statutory notifications.

precedents.event: R (Nur) v Birmingham City Council, failure to maintain lawful allocation scheme records
precedents.source: High Court of Justice (Administrative Court) [2023] EWHC 1801 (Admin)
precedents.shows: The High Court found unlawful systemic administration where a council failed to operate its published allocation policy transparently, leaving applicants in severe housing need unable to track or enforce their rightful priority banding.

walkthrough.actor: Khadija Al-Hassan, and the silent queue downgrade
walkthrough.narrative: Under traditional municipal housing databases, priority points and banding levels are internal database fields updated during routine administrative maintenance, data migrations, or automated review sweeps. When a family's priority band is removed or lowered without notice, no paper trail is delivered to the applicant; the discovery only occurs weeks or months later when portal bids fail to register near the top of shortlist queues. Because Housing Act 1996 section 202 review requests must strictly be lodged within twenty-one days of decision notification, silent administrative updates effectively extinguish the statutory right to review before the family realizes an adverse decision has been made.

Oakhaven commits its housing allocations register to an append-only transparency log. The authority establishes a strict operational invariant: every assignment of an applicant reference, allocation band, priority award, or re-assessment must be published as a signed log entry referencing the statutory criteria under Housing Act 1996 section 166A.

body.title: Oakhaven Housing Allocation Register Scheme 2026
body.rules: Housing Act 1996 Part VI; Oakhaven Allocations Policy v4

walkthrough.narrative: Khadija submits a medical assessment report from her daughter's NHS pediatric consultant certifying severe chronic asthma worsened by damp temporary accommodation, meeting the statutory threshold for medical priority under the published policy.

The medical assessment officer confirms Khadija's entitlement to Band 1 (Urgent Medical Priority). The authority logs the priority band assignment on the transparency log, providing Khadija with a cryptographic receipt that records the exact date, assessment citation, and awarded priority band.

body.statutory_basis: Housing Act 1996 s.166A(3)(b) (medical and welfare grounds)

walkthrough.narrative: Six months later, an automated IT batch clean-up job reviews all open cases older than ninety days and attempts to downgrade applications without logged re-assessments to Band 3. Because the system is bound to the append-only log, it cannot alter Khadija's records in place; it must publish an explicit transition event stating the downgrade and triggering an immediate notification to the applicant and independent witnesses.

Khadija's client application detects the logged downgrade event on the transparency log and alerts her immediately, before the twenty-one-day statutory review window under Housing Act 1996 section 202 has elapsed. With support from the local law centre, she submits a formal challenge citing the verified medical evidence from the log and demanding reinstatement.

The senior housing manager reviews the case, identifies that the automated batch downgrade occurred without an updated clinical reassessment, and logs a corrective determination reinstating Khadija to Band 1 with full backdated queue priority.

body.reason: Administrative review upheld: medical priority criteria sustained under Housing Act 1996 s.202 review

walkthrough.actor: Oakhaven Law Centre and Tenant Representatives
walkthrough.narrative: The law centre independently audits the public transparency log. By analyzing the published event chain without viewing private medical data, auditors verify that all batch modifications are visible, that unreasoned downgrades are flagged, and that queue positions are calculated from unalterable cryptographic commitments. The protocol successfully eliminates silent administrative attrition, though structural housing scarcity remains.

protection_plain: Every modification of applicant banding or housing queue standing must cite statutory grounds and be committed to an append-only log with contemporaneous written reasons.
verdict_plain: An append-only log prevents silent automated downgrades and enforces review rights, but cannot manufacture social housing stock to eliminate structural waiting times.

findings.observation: An unreasoned batch update cannot be committed secretly when all status transitions require a cited rule and a signed log entry, protecting statutory review windows.
The protocol guarantees that queue ordering and priority awards are incorruptible and auditable, but cannot solve the structural scarcity of available homes (refusal 11).
